svg.title: A limit that exists is not a limit that binds
svg.desc: Three ways a payment limit fails, the single cause they share, and the four things that make a limit bind.
svg.text: A limit that exists is not a limit that binds
Every control asked whether the payment was permitted.
None of them asked how much could leave, or who owned that number.
THREE WAYS A LIMIT FAILS
The limit was set above the loss
A ceiling high enough to clear legitimate settlement and payroll is
high enough to bound nothing.
The limit lived in a policy, not in the engine
If the ceiling lives inside the provider's platform, a compromised
provider is enforcing compromised limits.
The limit was attached to the wrong object
A ceiling on the channel rather than on the class of payment bounds
the door, not the money that walks through it.
All three are the same failure wearing different clothes.
The number was never owned by anyone who had the evidence
to set it, and to say that holding a payment was correct.
WHAT MAKES IT BIND

g.text: Enforce the limit in the engine, not the policy
It has to sit on the bank's side of the trust boundary.
Add the period total, and be honest about what it does
It makes the attack a pacing problem. It does not cap the incident.
Keep ordinary payments out of the approval path
Past a few dozen per reviewer per day, approval becomes a rubber stamp.
Can one channel be cut this afternoon without stranding payments in flight?

svg.text: The control is not new and not optional: SWIFT CSCF transaction business controls and FFIEC wholesale payment
examination procedures both require it. The gap is not whether to have a limit, but whether it binds.
This is an argument about where the bound must sit. It is not an assessment of any institution's controls.
